analysis.one_liner: Raises wage, severance, and pension priority in bankruptcies and restricts executive bonuses during them.
analysis.headline: Introduced in the final two weeks of 2024, the bill never received a hearing or vote and died when that Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill rewrites federal bankruptcy law to favor workers and retirees when a company goes broke. It doubles the priority cap on unpaid wages, makes severance and benefit contributions payable ahead of general creditors, lets workers claim losses from failed pension plans and company stock in their 401(k)s, and makes it much harder for a bankrupt company to cut union contracts or retiree health benefits. It also restricts and claws back executive bonuses paid before or during a bankruptcy, and requires courts weighing a company sale to favor buyers who keep jobs and honor pensions.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers and retirees of companies that file for bankruptcy. They would get doubled priority on unpaid wages, priority for severance and benefit-plan contributions, new claims for pension shortfalls and lost 401(k) stock value, and stronger rights in negotiations over union contracts and retiree benefits. Unions would gain standing to file claims, recover fees, and stop debtors from forcing contract cuts while paying executives bonuses.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers and retirees of bankrupt companies

how_it_helps.text: Doubles the priority cap on unpaid wages and benefit contributions from $10,000 to $20,000 per worker and removes the 180-day lookback window, so more workers get paid ahead of general creditors [S2].
Makes severance pay and contributions to employee benefit plans priority expenses payable during the case, deemed fully earned when a worker is laid off [S2].
Gives WARN Act damages (pay owed for mass layoffs without required notice) priority status alongside wages, and makes unpaid post-filing wages a cost the secured lender's collateral must cover [S2].

Lets workers and retirees claim the shortfall when a defined-benefit pension is terminated and lets 401(k) participants claim losses on company stock held in their plan when the employer committed fraud or breached a duty [S2].

Makes it much harder to reject a union contract or cut retiree health benefits: proposals must be limited to minimum essential savings, must include management cost savings, courts must find the debtor met a clear-and-convincing standard, and paying executives bonus programs creates a presumption against approval [S2].
Requires courts to give substantial weight to job preservation in company sales and to approve the offer that best preserves jobs, employment terms, and pension and health obligations [S2].

Restricts insider and executive bonuses in bankruptcy (capping certain transfers to 2% of the workforce's median pay and 10% of a plan's funds for retention programs), requires court approval of executive pay as reasonable and no more than the 50th percentile of comparable industry pay, and lets the estate claw back compensation from board members when workers' pensions or contracts are cut [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Creditors, and especially secured lenders and companies that bought debt cheaply in distressed situations, would recover less because wage, severance, pension, and retiree claims would rank ahead of them and could come out of collateral. Executives, insiders, and consultants of bankrupt companies would face strict limits on bonuses and clawback of pay when labor obligations are cut. Companies generally could face higher borrowing costs if lenders price in the larger worker claims.

drawbacks.text: Bankrupt companies' debts are often bought by pension funds, insurers, and mutual funds that hold them indirectly on behalf of ordinary savers; moving workers ahead of those creditors would shrink their recoveries and could raise borrowing costs for all companies [S2].

Tightening the standards for rejecting a union contract could make reorganization of heavily unionized firms harder to confirm, pushing some cases toward liquidation rather than a restructured company that keeps some jobs [S2].

Strict limits on exit and retention bonuses could make it harder to keep and motivate the management a failing company needs during a turnaround, a tradeoff supporters would have to defend against the bill's own goal of preserving jobs [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers, the benefits are concrete and large: more of what they are owed gets paid, pension losses become claims, and union and retiree benefits become far harder to strip. The costs fall on creditors, including funds that hold the debt on behalf of ordinary savers, and could modestly raise borrowing costs economy-wide. The bill tilts sharply toward labor by design, and the strongest honest objection is that stricter bargaining-rejection rules and bonus limits could occasionally cost jobs in turnaround cases.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced, and with the session ending two weeks later, it never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Jerrold Nadler, with Rep. Lou Correa as the sole cosponsor, introduced the bill on December 19, 2024 [S1].
It was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the same day, and no further action was recorded before that Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S4].

As the final version of the bill's text shows, the proposal would have doubled the wage-priority cap, given workers priority for severance and pension-related claims, tightened the rules for rejecting union contracts and cutting retiree benefits, and limited or clawed back executive bonuses in bankruptcy [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that use bankruptcy to shed wage, pension, and retiree obligations, and the secured lenders and distressed-debt investors whose recoveries are untouched by the status quo.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Bankrupt companies' executives and their lenders

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and its only cosponsor were both House Democrats, and the bill was introduced into a Republican-controlled House that took no action before the session ended.

industries.note: Unpaid wages, severance, benefit contributions, and WARN Act damages would become priority claims and could come out of the lender's collateral, and workers' new pension and stock-loss claims would dilute recoveries for anyone holding the debt. These investors' interest in this bill runs against the workers standing ahead of them.

industries.industry: Corporate executives, insiders, and turnaround consultants of bankrupt companies
industries.note: The bill caps or bans bonus and incentive programs, requires court approval of executive pay against industry benchmarks, bars deferred-compensation plans from being assumed when pensions are terminated, and claws back pay from board members when labor obligations are cut.

Unions gain standing to file creditor claims, recover attorney fees, a 21-day negotiating window before any contract-rejection hearing, limits on how much workers can be asked to concede, and protection for union contracts under the Railway Labor Act.

Filing companies would face bigger worker claims and tighter executive-pay rules but also clearer rules favoring reorganization over liquidation and purchases that preserve jobs; the ultimate cost flows to their creditors and, indirectly, to borrowers generally.
